books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Corwin Amendment text verified against the National Archives (prologue.blogs.archives.gov, “Unratified Amendments: Protection of Slavery,” February 19, 2020) and the Congressional Globe, 36th Congress, 2nd Session, p. 1284. Buchanan's Fourth Annual Message, December 3, 1860, verified against Richardson's Messages and Papers of the Presidents, vol. 5 (civilwarcauses.org/buch.htm). '. . .' marks omitted text. Both public domain.
stimulus.text:
The Corwin Amendment, passed by Congress on March 2, 1861, proposed: “No amendment shall be made to the Constitution which will authorize or give to Congress the power to abolish or interfere, within any State, with the domestic institutions thereof, including that of persons held to labor or service by the laws of said State.”

President James Buchanan, in his annual message to Congress on December 3, 1860, argued: “. . . the election of any one of our fellow citizens to the office of President does not of itself afford just cause for dissolving the Union. . . . secession is neither more nor less than revolution.”

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Corwin Amendment is best understood as an attempt to

options.text: free the slaves in the border states.
options.misconception: The amendment would have protected slavery in the states, not freed anyone.

options.text: reassure the South that slavery was safe there.
give Congress power over slavery in the territories.
options.misconception: The amendment bars Congress from interfering with slavery in the states; it says nothing about the territories.

options.text: admit the seceded states back into the Union.
options.misconception: The amendment was a promise to the states still in the Union, not a plan for readmitting those that had left.

rationales.A: The amendment would have protected slavery in the states, not freed anyone.
rationales.B: By making it unconstitutional for Congress ever to abolish slavery in a state, the amendment offered the South a permanent guarantee. Background: it passed Congress in March 1861, after seven states had already seceded.
rationales.C: The amendment bars Congress from interfering with slavery in the states; it says nothing about the territories.
rationales.D: The amendment was a promise to the states still in the Union, not a plan for readmitting those that had left.
rationales.general:
1. Read what the amendment forbids: any future amendment letting Congress touch slavery in a state.
2. A ban on future change is a guarantee to the present.
3. Background: Lincoln himself said he had no objection to making the protection “express and irrevocable.”
4. The offer was real, and it still failed.
Remember: a guarantee only works if the side being reassured believes it — and the seceded states no longer did.
